And when Jalal al-Din saw
that no other hope was left to him,
he dismounted from his horse,
and kissed his household and his children while he wept, and they wept loudly.
Then he left them and mounted his horse,
and said to the horsemen, his companions:
"Whoever loves me,
let him follow me in life and in death!"
And he struck his horse,
and broke through the line of the Tatars,
and cast himself, while mounted, into the water.
Now when Genghis Khan saw these things,
he ran to the edge (shore) of the river,
and was looking on and marveling.
And some of the Mongols also wanted
to cast themselves into the water as well and pursue after him.
But the King of Kings did not let them,
rather, placing his hand over his mouth, he was saying to his sons:
"From a father like this,
it is right that a son be born!"
And to the nobles he was saying:
"One like this is worthy to be called a man!
For if this one has escaped this time,
many marvelous deeds will be displayed by him,
and one who is prudent will not be negligent concerning him."

Now that Jalal al-Din, when with a single sword, a spear, and a shield {OCR: ܤܪܪܐ for ܤܟܪܐ?} he had been saved from the water and the fire of the sword, along with only six horsemen who were able to cross,
remained there on the banks of the Gihon (Indus) for about two days,
until about fifty other horsemen gathered to him,
and they set out toward India.
And there also overtook him there about a hundred other horsemen of his own.
And they sent a scout before them,
and he went and scouted the land.
And he came and informed them
that two thousand of the force of the Indians were in a certain place.
And the Khwarazmians went and attacked them,
and they killed them all,
and took their horses.
And they grew in number and became about five hundred horsemen.
Then five thousand of the Indians gathered,
and came and encountered them,
and the Indians were broken again.
And when the rest of the Khwarazmians who had fled and were hidden in various places heard [this],
they desired and came to him,
and they became about three thousand.
And when the Indian kings saw that they did not have the strength of the Khwarazmians,
they made peace with the Khwarazmshah,
and sent him many gifts.
